title: Simplify Your Leadership Style: The Power of Subtraction (leadershipwithatwist.substack.com), November 5, 2026
author: Heather McGonigal
source: Leadership With a Twist, Empowering Leadership Teams
summary: Coach Heather McGonigal closes her simplification series by arguing that one of the best things a leader can do is stop trying to do quite so much. She notes that highly responsible, caring leaders often add commitments, processes and expectations from good intentions, and that the cost is the time, attention and energy that make presence and patience possible. Her central distinction is that being committed to doing good does not mean being committed to doing everything. A leader who is exhausted and rushing has little compassion or listening capacity left, whereas more room allows thinking before responding and bringing creativity and care to people. She frames simplification as an ongoing practice of noticing unnecessary complexity rather than a one-time project. The post ends with a seven-day experiment to subtract one unnecessary thing a day and to notice what the new space makes possible.
points: McGonigal separates doing good from doing everything, arguing that conscientious leaders overextend because of good intentions.
Overload erodes the patience, listening and compassion that leadership relies on, so subtraction is framed as a way to lead better rather than do less.
Simplicity is presented as a standing practice of recognizing added complexity and choosing differently, not a one-time cleanup.
The seven-day challenge asks leaders to subtract one unnecessary item daily and then observe what that space made possible.
Some of what is worth removing, she suggests, are self-imposed expectations that nobody else even knows about.
quotes: What if one of the best things we could do to become better leaders, better teammates, and even better humans was to stop trying to do quite so much?
Our time, attention, and energy are precious resources. And when we’re stretched too thin, we don’t always have much left to give to the things that matter most.

These are wonderful intentions, but being committed to doing good doesn’t mean we have to commit to doing everything. In fact, sometimes all that doing gets in the way of our ability to be fully present.

What kind of leader are you when you’re exhausted, distracted, and rushing from one responsibility to the next? How much patience and compassion do you have available for others when you’re running on empty?
Simplicity isn’t just about getting more done with less effort. It’s about creating the conditions for us to show up as our best selves.
But we can get better at recognizing when we’re adding unnecessary complexity and choosing a different path.
For the next seven days, experiment with finding one small opportunity each day to subtract something unnecessary from your life or work.
Remember, the goal isn’t to do it all. It’s to make room for a life, and a way of leading, that feels meaningful to you.
